entry.evidence: We revisit the question of MICI in the AIS using a more complex parameterization of cliff calving

sequences.source_document: Publisher XML text (jats_text) of the published paper, with PDF for figures

steps.action: The authors take up the marine ice-cliff instability concept from the published stress analysis of ice cliffs and from DeConto and Pollard.
steps.quote: This is referred to as Marine Ice Cliff Instability (MICI)

steps.action: They cite DeConto and Pollard's projection of up to 1 m per century and its criticism as an overestimate from an unconstrained step-like cliff-calving law.
steps.quote: However, this study has been criticized as over-estimating sea level contribution owing to a lack of observationally constrained models

steps.action: They pose the question of MICI speed and sea-level contribution in the WAIS under a shear-failure cliff-calving law.
steps.quote: We revisit the question of MICI in the AIS using a more complex parameterization of cliff calving

steps.action: They adopt, from their own earlier work, the hypothesis that calved icebergs form a mélange whose buttressing caps the calving rate.
steps.quote: we further assume that calved icebergs form an ice mélange that buttresses the ice cliffs, providing an upper bound on calving rates

steps.action: They use their earlier cliff-calving law (2019) and mélange-buttressing parameterization with the Cmax geometry formula (2021), and argue that the poorly constrained C0 matters little under buttressing.
steps.quote: The model for mélange-buttressed cliff calving consists of two parts: cliff-calving parameterization and mélange-buttressing parameterization

steps.action: They set mu0 and gamma as in earlier work and bound the exit velocity between observed mélange and iceberg drift speeds. They then compute Cmax for Thwaites, Pine Island and two extreme geometries from manually measured embayment trapezoids (Table 1).
steps.quote: by measuring the embayment manually

steps.action: They use the PISM regional WAIS setup and the 100 000-year spin-up of Feldmann et al. (2019) at 4 km resolution. The resolution is justified by the earlier MISMIP3d grounding-line reversibility tests.
steps.quote: At this resolution, the reversibility of the grounding line is similar to that of higher-order models

steps.action: They design the experiments: REF, BMT (200 m/a basal melt), FLK (floatkill of all Amundsen floating ice), CC# (fixed Cmax 2-20 km/a) and CCA# (adaptive Cmax for exit velocities 10-1000 km/a). They add a stand-alone mélange run with seasonal exit velocity to represent freezing.
steps.quote: Five types of experiments were carried out

steps.action: They run the MISI-only experiments FLK and BMT and obtain about 0.6 m of sea-level rise in 100 years.
steps.quote: the two MISI experiments (FLK and BMT) contribute about 0.6 m of sea-level rise within 100 a

steps.action: They compare the MISI result with the LARMIP-2 range and with the ABUMIP finding that floatkill and large basal melt give similar loss.
steps.quote: This corresponds to the upper limit of the sea-level contribution from the Amundsen sector found in LARMIP-2

steps.action: They vary the ice-shelf removal mechanism (floatkill versus imposed basal melt) and find nearly identical sea-level contributions.
steps.quote: The sea-level contributions resulting from the FLK and BMT experiments are very similar.

steps.action: They run the fixed-Cmax cliff-calving experiments. MICI adds up to 1.5 times the MISI contribution at low Cmax and doubles or triples it at 10-20 km/a, with calving amplification computed from the separately reported discharge.
steps.quote: MICI can more than double (CC10) or even triple (CC20) the sea-level contribution compared with the MISI experiments

steps.action: They vary the mélange exit velocity across the adaptive experiments. The sea-level contributions bracket those of the fixed-Cmax runs, and CCA1000 exceeds five times the MISI contribution.
steps.quote: The adaptive experiment with the largest exit velocity (CCA1000) has more than five times the sea-level contribution of the MISI experiments

steps.action: They attribute the barely faster retreat at small Cmax to PISM's subgrid partially-filled-cell scheme, citing unpublished channel sensitivity tests of the resolution dependence.
steps.quote: This is because PISM uses a subgrid scheme for the ice margin

steps.action: They read off the adaptive runs that Cmax falls with grounding-line retreat as the calving front lengthens and the embayments merge, to about one third of its initial value (Table 3).
steps.quote: the upper bound on calving rate decreases with grounding-line retreat into the Amundsen Basin

steps.action: They fit an exponential relation of normalized Cmax to sea-level contribution across the adaptive experiments (Eq. 3, Fig. 6).
steps.quote: The relation between calving rate and sea-level contribution can be fitted with

steps.action: They keep the claim that growing mélange buttressing lowers the calving bound so that MICI decelerates as it progresses.
steps.quote: MICI cannot be arbitrarily fast and even decelerates as it progresses

steps.action: They trace grounding-line retreat rates along Thwaites and Pine Island flowlines against bed topography (Figs. 7-9), noting stalls at ridges and acceleration on retrograde slopes.
steps.quote: Ridges in the bed topography at 220 and 430 km cause stagnation of grounding-line retreat on the upslope

steps.action: They derive the expectation that retreat rate should relate to bed depth, from the superlinear thickness scaling of grounding-line flux (Schoof) and of cliff calving.
steps.quote: We expect bed topography to control grounding-line retreat for two reasons

steps.action: They test the expectation with Spearman coefficients between bed depth and retreat rate (Table 4) and find weak correlation for Pine Island and none for Thwaites.
steps.quote: shows only a minimal correlation for Pine Island Glacier and no correlation at all for Thwaites Glacier

steps.action: They explain the failed correlation by auxiliaries rather than rejecting the expectation: a 1-D flowline embedded in 2-D flow, misaligned flowlines, and inertia of ice flow.
steps.quote: There are two main reasons for [...]

steps.action: They keep, on qualitative grounds, the claim that bed topography is a major control of the rate of grounding-line retreat.
steps.quote: So we can conclude that bed topography is a major control of the rate of grounding-line retreat.

steps.action: They run the stand-alone non-steady mélange model with zero and seasonal exit velocity. Zero exit velocity suppresses calving within about 10 years, while seasonal variation only modulates the calving rate.
steps.quote: Assuming that no mélange exits the embayment, mélange buildup can prevent calving almost completely within 10 a

steps.action: They note that the model result conflicts with Greenland observations of winter mélange freezing stopping calving, and attribute this to slow mélange equilibration.
steps.quote: Contrary to observations, in this simplified mélange parameterization, [...] freezing of mélange [...] calving.

steps.action: They check the mélange model's force per unit width when calving is suppressed against the 6.66e6 N/m backpressure threshold of Crawford et al. (2021).
steps.quote: In our solution of the non-steady-state equation, a similar force per unit width was found when calving is suppressed

steps.action: They keep the claim that mélange build-up can halt MICI only temporarily, in winter.
steps.quote: However, this is only likely to happen in the winter season and would therefore halt MICI only temporarily.

steps.action: They list the limitations of the idealized-geometry mélange parameterization (non-unique geometry, uniform calving, pinning points, external margin, freezing) and propose a spatially resolved mélange model.
steps.quote: it would be beneficial to use a spatially resolved mélange model

steps.action: They compare with the re-advance of Sermeq Kujalleq under ocean cooling and stronger mélange, inferring that regional climate can slow cliff-calving retreat.
steps.quote: This suggests that changes in regional climatic conditions may slow or prevent grounding-line retreat caused by cliff calving.

steps.action: They compare with plough-mark evidence that deglacial MICI stopped at a bathymetric ridge; the simulations show only temporary halts at interior ridges.
steps.quote: However, our simulations show only temporary halts in grounding-line retreat at bathymetric ridges in the interior of the WAIS

steps.action: They conclude that the lengthening calving front at a fixed exit width increases buttressing and slows MICI. They judge that mélange alone is unlikely to stop MICI but might enable ice-shelf regrowth.
steps.quote: a decrease in the upper bound on calving rates, and consequently a slowdown in the progress of MICI

sequences.source_document: Open discussion record of preprint tc-2021-238 (RC1, RC2, RC3, CC1 and author replies AC1-AC4)

steps.action: In response to RC1 ¶4 (sensitivity tests on u_ex) and RC3 ¶9-11 (focus on adaptive Cmax), the authors added the adaptive experiments CCA10, CCA50, CCA200 and CCA1000 alongside the original CCA100.
steps.quote: In order to deal with the uncertainety in the melange exit velocity uex, we performed additionally a range of adaptive experiments

steps.action: At RC1 ¶5's request, the authors added text on how C0, mu0, b0 and b1 were chosen, from earlier work and Amundson and Burton (2018).
steps.quote: Details have been added [...] .

steps.action: At RC1 ¶9-15's request, the authors added the spin-up length, a separate boundary-conditions section, the till-friction reference and a resolution statement.
steps.quote: Length of the spinup was added.

steps.action: At RC3 ¶12's request, the authors added the justification for assuming a mélange-filled embayment when estimating Cmax: the margin cannot evolve and thickness equilibrates in a few years.
steps.quote: Yes, there would be more calving, if the embayment was not filled with mélange.

steps.action: At RC1 ¶29's request, the authors added that the partially-filled-cell artifact depends on resolution, citing previously unpublished channel sensitivity tests.
steps.quote: Previous unpublished sensitivity tests in a channel setup showed

steps.action: RC1 ¶32 asked for the extended-run results; the authors added only 'not shown here' and did not show the results.
steps.quote: “not shown here” was added in the manuscript.

steps.action: At RC1 ¶38's request, the authors clarified that the mélange model can represent melting but not freezing, so freezing is represented by a vanishing exit velocity.
steps.quote: Therefore freezing is modelled by assuming a vanishing exit velocity.

steps.action: After RC1 ¶36 and RC3 ¶14, the authors reversed the claim in the section title on mélange freezing and moved the section into Methods and Results.
steps.quote: The title was corrected to “ [...] is not sufficient to [...] ”.

steps.action: In response to RC1 ¶46, the authors explained the late rise in calving amplification by the grounding line reaching the edge of the calving domain, and adapted the plot ranges.
steps.quote: The calving amplification of the CC20 and the CCA1000 experiments increases toward the end of the simulation time

steps.action: In response to RC3 ¶13, the authors added the caveat that ice-divide movement may shift the true flowline, which the analysis does not account for.
steps.quote: It may be that, due to movement of the ice divide, the actual flowline, aka main direction of the ice flow, changes.

steps.action: In response to RC3 ¶18, the authors corrected the mechanism statement: Cmax falls because the front-to-exit distance grows, not because the embayment widens.
steps.quote: The distance between the calving front and the embayment exit increases. This has been corrected.

steps.action: Commenter CC1 ¶6 asked for a numerical convergence study. The authors acknowledged non-convergence at 4 km, did no new test, and relied on Feldmann et al. (2014).
steps.quote: We know that the model is not converged at a resolution of 4km.

steps.action: Commenter CC1 ¶5 asked for observational tests of the model. The authors argued such a test is not currently feasible and did no new work.
steps.quote: Since the cliff- calving parametrisation underestimates calving rates of current glaciers, another calving parametrisation would need to be used

steps.action: RC2 objected to the MISI/MICI framing, the ad hoc parameterizations, the 4 km resolution and the contradiction between the Section 3.4 title and its correlation result. The authors gave no point-by-point response, and the Section 3.4 title stayed.
steps.quote: We find it difficult to respond to this text since it is unclear to us what the purpose of the text is.

end.claim: In the adaptive PISM experiments, mélange buttressing strengthens as the grounding line retreats into the Amundsen Basin. The calving upper bound falls to about one third of its initial value (fitted against sea-level contribution, Eq. 3, up to about 0.5 m), slowing MICI.

decisive_move.sentence: The claim rests on re-estimating Cmax every 5 model years from the evolving embayment geometry in the adaptive experiments; without this step no slowdown of MICI would appear.

gates.evidence: No data were acquired: the mélange-buttressing hypothesis (inherited) directed the design of the adaptive simulations, and the exit-velocity sweep was added after review. The slowdown claim could in principle have failed to appear, but it follows closely from the geometry dependence built into Eq. 1. The one explicit test, the bed-depth versus retreat-rate correlation, failed, and the claim was kept on qualitative grounds. Nothing was fixed in advance.

imports.item: Spearman rank correlation between bed depth and grounding-line retreat rate
internal friction coefficient of a granular mélange (quasi-static granular flow)
Mohr-Coulomb plastic till model for basal friction

limits: Composition none_fits: the paper is a simulation sensitivity study. Inherited parameterizations are applied to realistic geometry and the forcing is varied, but no rivals face a crucial test, and conditions are neither found nor repeated by nature. The authors disclaim quantitative relevance (§0 ¶1). Sub-claim statuses: the MISI contribution of 0.6 m in 100 years and the MICI doubling or tripling are conditional scenario results with no stated uncertainty, closest to estimate_with_resolution without resolution. 'Bed topography is a major control' is kept as a qualitative regularity after its statistical test failed (§3.4 ¶8-9), so its status is effectively none. 'Winter freezing is not sufficient to stop MICI' is a model result the authors say contradicts observations, which they attribute to the parameterization. Mélange may enable ice-shelf regrowth (§5 ¶4) is untested speculation. The paper reports no numerical convergence test; the authors admitted in review that the model is not converged at 4 km (inference from AC3-S p.1). The resolution dependence of the subgrid artifact rests on unpublished tests. Cmax values for the fixed runs were chosen ad hoc (authors' word in AC1-S p.2). Embayment geometry was measured manually. Output data are available only on request. RC3's suggestion to move the constant-Cmax runs out of the main text was not adopted. The review record shows that the CCA10-CCA1000 runs and the reversed freezing claim were added after review; the published text does not disclose this.

disagreements.target: DeConto and Pollard (2016) step-like cliff-calving parameterization
disagreements.support: The paper replaces the step function with an exponential shear-failure law capped by mélange buttressing, and shows that the MICI contribution depends strongly on the cap.
disagreements.quote: parameterized cliff calving with a step-like function that is zero for ice cliffs below the stability limit

disagreements.target: DeConto and Pollard (2016): hydrofracturing as main mechanism of ice-shelf breakup
disagreements.support: Cited projections (Trusel et al. 2015) put Pine Island surface melt far below the collapse threshold even under RCP8.5, and Robel and Banwell show anomalous melt is needed.
disagreements.quote: Therefore, it is unlikely that the ice shelves in the Amundsen region will fail owing to hydrofracturing.

disagreements.target: Pollard et al. (2015) assumption that small ice-shelf remnants do not prevent cliff calving
disagreements.support: The Schoof flux may not apply beyond flowline setups (Reese et al. 2018b), and a small shelf may affect the cliff stress balance in 3-D.
disagreements.quote: they assumed that a small ice-shelf remnant with vanishing buttressing strength does not prevent cliff calving

disagreements.target: Wise et al. (2017): deglacial MICI stopped at a prominent bathymetric ridge
disagreements.support: The simulations show only temporary halts at interior bathymetric ridges.
disagreements.quote: However, our simulations show only temporary halts in grounding-line retreat at bathymetric ridges in the interior of the WAIS

disagreements.target: Interpretation of Sermeq Kujalleq retreat as the onset of a cliff-calving regime (Bassis and Walker 2011; DeConto and Pollard 2016; [...]
disagreements.support: Cited observations of re-advance since 2016 under ocean cooling and increased mélange buttressing (Khazendar et al. 2019; Joughin et al. 2020).
disagreements.quote: However, since 2016, Sermeq Kujalleq has re-advanced as a result of regional ocean cooling

alternatives_considered.chosen: floatkill removal of all Amundsen floating ice for the MICI experiments
alternatives_considered.reason: basal melt leaves ice-shelf remnants of a few grid cells that prevent MICI onset in PISM

alternatives_considered.chosen: exponential shear-failure cliff-calving law (Schlemm and Levermann 2019)
alternatives_considered.alternatives: step-like function of DeConto and Pollard (2016)
alternatives_considered.reason: more complex parameterization based on shear failure, supported by Crawford et al. (2021)

alternatives_considered.chosen: both fixed upper bounds (CC2-CC20) and geometry-adaptive upper bounds (CCA10-CCA1000)
alternatives_considered.alternatives: fixed Cmax 2, 5, 10, 20 km/a; adaptive Cmax with exit velocity 10, 50, 100, 200, 1000 km/a
alternatives_considered.reason: exit velocity lies within the range bounded by observed mélange and iceberg drift speeds

alternatives_considered.chosen: embayment assumed entirely filled with mélange
alternatives_considered.reason: the parameterization cannot evolve the mélange margin, and mélange thickness equilibrates within a few years

alternatives_considered.chosen: cliff calving only at exposed grounded ice cliffs
alternatives_considered.alternatives: cliff calving also behind small ice-shelf remnants (Pollard et al. 2015)
alternatives_considered.reason: the Schoof flux may not apply beyond a flowline setup; a small shelf may impact the cliff stress balance in 3-D

alternatives_considered.chosen: mélange freezing represented by a seasonal exit velocity falling to zero
alternatives_considered.reason: the mélange parameterization cannot explicitly model freezing

alternatives_considered.alternatives: spatially resolved mélange model (e.g. Pollard et al. 2018)
alternatives_considered.reason: such a model introduces additional mélange parameters, which are difficult to constrain
